chapterTitle: Web Server Configuration with Nginx and Apache
aiGenerationNote:

The next 5 minutes will show Nginx server blocks for static content and a reverse proxy, including `proxy_pass` and `proxy_set_header` directives. screens.title: Web Server Configuration with Nginx and Apache
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to configure and secure two ubiquitous Linux web servers: Apache and Nginx. We focus on practical tasks you will do as an LFCE: creating virtual hosts or server blocks to host multiple sites, obtaining and installing SSL/TLS certificates with certbot, and using Nginx as a reverse proxy to forward traffic to backend applications. You will see real configuration examples, the commands to validate syntax, and a hands-on scenario pairing a static site with a proxied Node. js app. Why this matters: correct web server configuration protects data in transit, isolates sites on a host, and lets you centralize logging and TLS termination. A frequent pitfall is misconfigured virtual host names or blocked ports, which prevents certificates from being issued or HTTP requests from mapping to the intended site. By the end you will know where Apache and Nginx store configs, how certbot performs automatic renewal, and which headers to forward so your backend sees the real client IP. Think about a service you manage: can it respond securely and show real client addresses in its logs?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives target the concrete skills you will practice. First, you will configure virtual hosts in Apache and server blocks in Nginx so a single IP answers multiple domain names. That skill matters because misconfigured host names often route traffic to the wrong site. Second, you will install and use certbot to obtain Let's Encrypt certificates, enable HTTPS, and set up automated renewal. You will learn common failures like DNS A records or closed firewall ports that stop issuance. Third, you will master core web server directives used for content serving, redirection, and access control — directives that determine which files are served, how requests are rewritten, and who can read a directory. Finally, you will understand how to configure Nginx as a reverse proxy, forwarding requests to backend apps, and using proxy_set_header directives so the backend sees correct client information. Each objective is paired with a small verification milestone so you can demonstrate competency by reloading the server, running syntax checks, and confirming HTTPS and header propagation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Lab Tasks and Diagnostics
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on lab tasks and diagnostic skills you will need. First, you will perform syntax checks and reload servers safely using commands like nginx -t and apachectl configtest. This habit prevents downtime caused by invalid configurations. Second, you will resolve permission and SELinux issues so the web server user can access DocumentRoot and write logs. You will practice chown and restorecon commands described in the lab. Third, you will validate firewall and DNS settings so certbot can complete domain validation; understanding that blocked ports or wrong A records prevent certificate issuance is crucial. Fourth, you will complete the chapter hands-on scenario: set up one static site and one proxied application on Nginx, enable HTTPS for both, and confirm that HTTP redirects to HTTPS. Each card ends with a verified competency milestone so you can confirm site reachability, certificate validity, and correct header propagation. These diagnostics are essential real-world skills that reduce outages and speed recovery.

screens.title: Apache configuration and virtual hosts
screens.narratorSegment: Apache remains a flexible, module-driven web server. As an LFCE you must know where its main configuration lives and how virtual hosts are defined. On RHEL/CentOS the primary file is /etc/httpd/conf/httpd. conf; on Debian/Ubuntu it's /etc/apache2/apache2. conf. Virtual host definitions are typically stored in /etc/httpd/conf. d/ or /etc/apache2/sites-available and enabled via symlink in sites-enabled. A VirtualHost block binds an IP:port and maps ServerName to a DocumentRoot; that root is the directory Apache serves. For example, a VirtualHost for www. example. com sets ServerAdmin, ServerName, DocumentRoot, and log files, and often includes a Directory block controlling Options and AllowOverride. Practically, misplacing ServerName or forgetting to enable the site causes requests to fall back to the first virtual host defined. Always run apachectl configtest before reload to catch syntax errors. Concrete example: create /var/www/example. com/html with index. html, ensure ownership and permissions let the apache user read files, then enable the vhost and reload. A common misconception is thinking DocumentRoot ownership must be root: instead ensure the web server user can read files, but avoid giving unnecessary write access. Key takeaway: correct file locations, enabling sites, and syntax checks prevent downtime and wrong-site responses.

keyIdea.title: Apache essentials
keyIdea.text: VirtualHost blocks plus correct ServerName and enabled site files determine which site responds; always validate syntax and permissions before reloading.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Apache Virtual Hosts
Canonical VirtualHost example
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerAdmin webmaster@example.com
    ServerName www.example.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/example.com/html
    ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/example.com_error.log
    CustomLog /var/log/httpd/example.com_access.log combined

    <Directory /var/www/example.com/html>
        Options Indexes FollowSymLinks
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>

# Enable site on Debian/Ubuntu: sudo a2ensite example.com.conf
# Then: sudo systemctl reload apache2
Example
Create /var/www/example.com/html/index.html, set chown and chmod so the web user can read files, enable the vhost and reload Apache.
Common mistake
If ServerName is missing or mis-typed, Apache serves the first VirtualHost defined. Confirm the ServerName directive and enabled site symlink.
Key Takeaway

Define ServerName, set DocumentRoot ownership and permissions, test configuration with apachectl configtest, then reload safely.

Explanation & checklist
  • Know typical config paths: /etc/httpd/ or /etc/apache2/ and sites-available/sites-enabled on Debian systems.
  • Use directory blocks to control overrides, indexes, and access permissions.
  • Log file paths help when diagnosing startup or runtime errors.
  • Run apachectl configtest to avoid syntax errors on reload.
Quick permission commands
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/example.com
sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/example.com

screens.title: Nginx server blocks and static site hosting
screens.narratorSegment: Nginx is designed for high concurrency and efficient static file serving. Its configuration uses server blocks to map server_name to a root directory and to define access and logging. Typical files live in /etc/nginx/nginx. conf with server blocks in /etc/nginx/conf. d or sites-available. A minimal server block lists listen, server_name, root and an index. The location / block commonly uses try_files to prefer real files and fall back to returning 404. For example, a server block for www. example. com sets root /var/www/example. com/html and access and error log paths. After creating the block test it with nginx -t and reload with systemctl reload nginx. A concrete lab step is to create the document root, add index. html, set ownership to nginx or www-data depending on distro, then confirm curl http://localhost returns the page. A common misconception is copying an Apache Directory directive into Nginx — Nginx handles access rules differently via location and directive scopes. Key takeaway: Nginx server blocks are simple and fast for static assets; always validate syntax and file permissions before relying on them in production.

keyIdea.title: Nginx basics
keyIdea.text: Server blocks define host behavior; try_files and location directives determine how requests map to files, and nginx -t safeguards changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Nginx Server Blocks
Nginx server block example
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name www.example.com example.com;
    root /var/www/example.com/html;
    index index.html index.htm;

    access_log /var/log/nginx/example.com_access.log;
    error_log /var/log/nginx/example.com_error.log;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ =404;
    }
}

# Enable on Debian/Ubuntu: sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/example.com.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
# Then: sudo systemctl reload nginx
Example
After creating the root and index file, run nginx -t to validate syntax and then systemctl reload nginx. Use curl or a browser to confirm the page loads.
Explanation and notes
  • listen binds to a port; server_name maps requests to this block.
  • root points to the filesystem path that serves files; index lists default files.
  • try_files helps avoid directory indexing and returns 404 if not found.
  • Use nginx -t before reload to catch errors and avoid downtime.
Key Takeaway

Nginx server blocks are concise. Validate syntax and set correct ownership so the worker user can read static files.

screens.title: Obtain and install SSL/TLS with Let's Encrypt and certbot
screens.narratorSegment: Securing web traffic with HTTPS is essential. Let's Encrypt provides free certificates and certbot automates obtaining and installing them for Apache and Nginx. The typical flow is: ensure your domain's A record points to the server and that ports 80 and 443 are open; install certbot and the appropriate plugin for your web server; run certbot with the server plugin and domain flags; verify automatic renewal is configured. For Nginx the command is certbot --nginx -d www. example. com -d example. com; for Apache use certbot --apache. Certbot will perform domain validation by reaching your server on port 80, then it will modify server configuration to reference certificate paths and enable HTTPS. Common failures include incorrect DNS, a firewall blocking validation ports, or an existing server block that conflicts with certbot's modifications. After installation, test certificate renewal with certbot renew --dry-run and inspect cron or systemd timers that call renewals. A practical example: after running certbot --nginx, confirm server listens on 443, check the certificate files under /etc/letsencrypt/live, and verify the browser shows a valid HTTPS connection. A common misconception is that certbot automatically fixes every server misconfiguration; in practice you must resolve DNS and conflicting configs first.

keyIdea.text: Certbot automates issuance and installation but depends on reachable DNS and open ports; always validate with dry-run and check renewal tasks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › SSL/TLS with Certbot
Command examples
# For Nginx
sudo certbot --nginx -d www.example.com -d example.com

# For Apache
sudo certbot --apache -d www.example.com -d example.com

# Test renewal
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
After certbot runs, it updates server configuration to reference /etc/letsencrypt/live/domain/fullchain.pem and privkey.pem, and it may add redirects from HTTP to HTTPS.
Verification checklist
  • Confirm A records point to server public IP.
  • Open ports 80 and 443 in firewall and cloud security groups.
  • Run nginx -t or apachectl configtest before certbot to avoid conflicts.
  • Check /etc/letsencrypt/live for certificate files and permissions.
Common failure
If DNS points elsewhere or ports are blocked, certbot cannot validate the domain and will fail to issue a certificate.
Key Takeaway

Certbot automates TLS but depends on reachable DNS and open ports; always dry-run renewals and inspect certificate locations after issuance.

screens.title: Nginx as a reverse proxy
screens.narratorSegment: Using Nginx as a reverse proxy centralizes TLS termination and allows backend applications to run without direct exposure. The proxy pattern: Nginx receives HTTPS requests, decrypts them, and forwards plain HTTP to a backend app. In a typical setup Nginx listens on 443 with ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key pointing to certbot-managed files, then uses proxy_pass to forward to localhost:3000 or another upstream. It is essential to forward headers like Host, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For so the backend sees the original client address and protocol. Without these headers, backend logs and logic may record requests as coming from 127.0.0.1. Also include proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme when the backend needs to know whether the original request was HTTPS. A concrete example is an app on port 3000 receiving proxied traffic; add the proxy_set_header lines to preserve client identity. Misconceptions include thinking proxy_pass changes the client's IP; it does not unless headers are set. Key takeaway: set headers and test the backend can read them, or client IPs will be lost in logs and analytics. Nginx as a reverse proxy means nginx can terminate tls and forward requests; use proxy_set_header directives so the backend receives the original client information.. In practical terms, ssl termination, proxy_pass, and forwarding client headers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Nginx can terminate TLS and forward requests; use proxy_set_header directives so the backend receives the original client information.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Reverse Proxy
Nginx reverse proxy example
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name app.example.com;

    ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/app.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/app.example.com/privkey.pem;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}
Why headers matter
  • Host: ensures backend knows which hostname the client used.
  • X-Real-IP: carries the immediate client IP to backend logs.
  • X-Forwarded-For: lists client and proxy chain IPs for chained proxies.
  • X-Forwarded-Proto: tells the backend whether the original request used HTTPS.
Common pitfall
If you forget to set X-Real-IP or X-Forwarded-For, backend logs show 127.0.0.1 and analytics or rate-limiting may misbehave.
Key Takeaway

Use Nginx to centralize TLS and forward original client headers so backend services can log and act on true client addresses.

screens.title: Hands-on: static site and proxied Node.js app
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough builds the lab: one static site and one proxied Node. js application. Start by creating document roots: /var/www/static. example. com/html and /var/www/app. example. com/html. Place an index. html into the static root. For the backend create a minimal Node. js app that listens on 127.0.0.1:3000 and responds with a simple message. Run the app in the background, then create two Nginx server blocks: one for static. example. com serving files directly, and another for app. example. com that proxy_passes to the Node. js port. After writing the configs, test nginx -t and reload. Finally use certbot --nginx to obtain certificates for both domains. The critical points: ensure file ownership allows the Nginx worker to read static files, ensure the Node app binds to localhost so it is not exposed directly, and confirm that proxy_set_header directives are present so the app receives client IPs and the protocol. A typical mistake is forgetting to run the Node app or binding it to 0.0.0.0, which may expose it unnecessarily. Confirm success by curling both hostnames and checking HTTPS and redirects. Hands-on: static site and proxied Node.js app means create two server blocks, run a local node.js backend on 127.0.0.1:3000, and secure both sites with certbot to complete the hands-on scenario.. In practical terms, file layout, minimal node.js app, and nginx server blocks for both sites. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab recipe
keyIdea.text: Create two server blocks, run a local Node.js backend on 127.0.0.1:3000, and secure both sites with certbot to complete the hands-on scenario.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Lab Walkthrough
Node.js minimal app (save as app.js)
// /var/www/app.example.com/html/app.js
const http = require('http');
const port = 3000;
const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
  res.statusCode = 200;
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
  res.end('Hello from Node.js backend!
');
});
server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1', () => {
  console.log(`Server running at http://127.0.0.1:${port}/`);
});

# Run in background: node /var/www/app.example.com/html/app.js &
Run the app bound to 127.0.0.1 to avoid exposing the backend directly. Then create Nginx server blocks and validate.
Nginx server blocks (static + proxy)
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name static.example.com;
    root /var/www/static.example.com/html;
    index index.html;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name app.example.com;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    }
}

# Test: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
# Then obtain certificates: sudo certbot --nginx -d static.example.com -d app.example.com
Pro tip
Use /etc/hosts for local testing or set DNS A records to your server IP for real domain validation by certbot.
Key Takeaway

Bind backends to localhost, set proxy headers, test configs, and obtain certificates to complete the lab setup securely.

screens.title: Apache vs Nginx: when to choose each
screens.narratorSegment: Both Apache and Nginx are powerful, but they excel at different tasks. Apache is modular and feature-rich with a long history, making it suitable when you rely on dynamic modules, per-directory. htaccess overrides, or complex rewrites via mod_rewrite. Nginx is event-driven and optimized for high concurrency and static file delivery; it is commonly used as a reverse proxy, load balancer, or cache in front of application servers. In practice, you might use Nginx to terminate TLS and forward to Apache for legacy applications, or choose pure Nginx when low memory and high throughput matter. A common misconception is that one server is always superior; instead, choose based on your app's needs. Example: a high-traffic static asset site benefits from Nginx's performance, while a legacy PHP app relying on many Apache modules may be easier to migrate with Apache. When designing a deployment, consider TLS termination, logging centralization, and whether your backend requires client IPs — if so configure X-Forwarded headers. Key takeaway: pick the server that aligns with workload characteristics and operational constraints, or combine them for best results. Apache

  • Good fit for legacy deployments with rich module usage.

screens.title: Diagnosing syntax, log, firewall and permission issues
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting web servers follows a predictable pattern: validate configuration syntax, inspect logs, confirm file permissions, and check network rules. Start with syntax checks: run nginx -t or apachectl configtest to catch parsing errors. If the server fails to start or reload, examine error logs at /var/log/nginx/error. log or /var/log/httpd/error_log to find line numbers and directives causing the failure. Permissions problems often manifest as 403 errors; verify ownership and read permissions for DocumentRoot and log directories and adjust with chown and chmod as needed. On RHEL/CentOS, SELinux can block access even with correct permissions; use restorecon -Rv on your DocumentRoot and setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1 when Nginx must connect to upstream services. Network checks involve ensuring firewall allows HTTP and HTTPS; use firewall-cmd or iptables rules to permit services and then reload. A practical diagnostic flow: run syntax test, tail the error log while reproducing the request, confirm permissions and SELinux context, then verify firewall and DNS. A common misconception is chasing code bugs before confirming that configuration or environment prevents the request from reaching the backend. Close with testing the fix and reloading safely.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Troubleshooting Checklist
Quick commands
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx

sudo apachectl configtest
sudo systemctl reload apache2

# Tail logs
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log
sudo tail -f /var/log/httpd/error_log
Permissions & SELinux
Set ownership so the web user reads files: sudo chown -R nginx:nginx /var/www/site. Use sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www to correct SELinux contexts and setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1 for reverse proxying needs.
Firewall
Ensure ports 80 and 443 are open. Example: firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent; --add-service=https --permanent; then firewall-cmd --reload.
Key Takeaway

Follow a structured debug flow: syntax checks, logs, permissions/SELinux, then network and DNS. This order saves time and reduces risk of cascading changes.

screens.title: Common assessment scenarios and diagnostic questions
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks two assessment scenarios derived from the chapter. Scenario one: two virtual hosts on Apache, but requests for the second domain return the first site's content. Diagnosis steps: check that the second VirtualHost file includes the correct ServerName directive and that the site is enabled (symlink in sites-enabled on Debian/Ubuntu). Run apachectl configtest and reload Apache if there are no errors. Also verify that the desired VirtualHost appears before others in the ordering if NameVirtualHost conflicts exist. The key principle is Apache matches the best defined server name, and it falls back to the first defined host when it cannot find a match. Scenario two: backend application logs show client IPs as 127.0.0.1 while Nginx proxies requests. Diagnosis steps: inspect the Nginx server block for proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr and proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; add them if missing and reload Nginx. Confirm the backend reads those headers and not the source connection IP. These scenarios test your ability to read configs, run syntax checks, and apply targeted fixes instead of broad restarts. Common assessment scenarios and diagnostic questions means diagnose wrong-site responses by checking servername and enabled vhost files; diagnose missing client ips by verifying proxy_set_header directives.. Steps: check ServerName in the suspect VirtualHost file, confirm the site is enabled, run apachectl configtest, examine vhost ordering, and verify DocumentRoot paths. The root cause is typically a missing or incorrect ServerName so Apache selects the first vhost by default.
Scenario 2 — Backend sees 127.0.0.1
Steps: inspect Nginx config for proxy_set_header X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For, add missing headers, reload Nginx, and verify the backend reads those headers. Without these headers the backend only sees the proxy's connection address.

screens.title: Operational best practices for production web servers
screens.narratorSegment: Operationalizing web servers in production requires repeatable practices. Always validate configuration changes with nginx -t or apachectl configtest and use graceful reloads to avoid downtime. Automate certificate renewal and monitor certificates so they never expire unexpectedly; certbot sets a timer or cron, and you should confirm it with certbot renew --dry-run. Centralize logs and rotate them to keep disk usage under control and to allow quick forensic analysis. Practice least privilege: the web server user should have only read access to DocumentRoot and write access to log directories; avoid leaving writable file permissions on site folders. When reverse proxying, terminate TLS at the edge and keep internal traffic on a private network when possible. For SELinux-enabled systems, include SELinux context changes in your deployment scripts so restores and policies survive reboots. Finally, document your server blocks and certificate locations so on-call engineers can respond quickly. A misconception is focusing only on feature configuration; operational checks and automation prevent outages. Key takeaway: validate, automate, monitor, and use least privilege to keep web services robust. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to configure and secure two ubiquitous Linux web servers: Apache and Nginx. We focus on practical tasks you will do as an LFCE: creating virtual hosts or server blocks to host multiple sites, obtaining and installing SSL/TLS certificates with certbot, and using Nginx as a reverse proxy to forward traffic to backend applications. You will see real configuration examples, the commands to validate syntax, and a hands-on scenario pairing a static site with a proxied Node. js app. Why this matters: correct web server configuration protects data in transit, isolates sites on a host, and lets you centralize logging and TLS termination. A frequent pitfall is misconfigured virtual host names or blocked ports, which prevents certificates from being issued or HTTP requests from mapping to the intended site. By the end you will know where Apache and Nginx store configs, how certbot performs automatic renewal, and which headers to forward so your backend sees the real client IP. Think about a service you manage: can it respond securely and show real client addresses in its logs?

These objectives target the concrete skills you will practice. First, you will configure virtual hosts in Apache and server blocks in Nginx so a single IP answers multiple domain names. That skill matters because misconfigured host names often route traffic to the wrong site. Second, you will install and use certbot to obtain Let's Encrypt certificates, enable HTTPS, and set up automated renewal. You will learn common failures like DNS A records or closed firewall ports that stop issuance. Third, you will master core web server directives used for content serving, redirection, and access control — directives that determine which files are served, how requests are rewritten, and who can read a directory. Finally, you will understand how to configure Nginx as a reverse proxy, forwarding requests to backend apps, and using proxy_set_header directives so the backend sees correct client information. Each objective is paired with a small verification milestone so you can demonstrate competency by reloading the server, running syntax checks, and confirming HTTPS and header propagation.

This second objectives screen focuses on lab tasks and diagnostic skills you will need. First, you will perform syntax checks and reload servers safely using commands like nginx -t and apachectl configtest. This habit prevents downtime caused by invalid configurations. Second, you will resolve permission and SELinux issues so the web server user can access DocumentRoot and write logs. You will practice chown and restorecon commands described in the lab. Third, you will validate firewall and DNS settings so certbot can complete domain validation; understanding that blocked ports or wrong A records prevent certificate issuance is crucial. Fourth, you will complete the chapter hands-on scenario: set up one static site and one proxied application on Nginx, enable HTTPS for both, and confirm that HTTP redirects to HTTPS. Each card ends with a verified competency milestone so you can confirm site reachability, certificate validity, and correct header propagation. These diagnostics are essential real-world skills that reduce outages and speed recovery.

Apache remains a flexible, module-driven web server. As an LFCE you must know where its main configuration lives and how virtual hosts are defined. On RHEL/CentOS the primary file is /etc/httpd/conf/httpd. conf; on Debian/Ubuntu it's /etc/apache2/apache2. conf. Virtual host definitions are typically stored in /etc/httpd/conf. d/ or /etc/apache2/sites-available and enabled via symlink in sites-enabled. A VirtualHost block binds an IP:port and maps ServerName to a DocumentRoot; that root is the directory Apache serves. For example, a VirtualHost for www. example. com sets ServerAdmin, ServerName, DocumentRoot, and log files, and often includes a Directory block controlling Options and AllowOverride. Practically, misplacing ServerName or forgetting to enable the site causes requests to fall back to the first virtual host defined. Always run apachectl configtest before reload to catch syntax errors. Concrete example: create /var/www/example. com/html with index. html, ensure ownership and permissions let the apache user read files, then enable the vhost and reload. A common misconception is thinking DocumentRoot ownership must be root: instead ensure the web server user can read files, but avoid giving unnecessary write access. Key takeaway: correct file locations, enabling sites, and syntax checks prevent downtime and wrong-site responses.

Nginx is designed for high concurrency and efficient static file serving. Its configuration uses server blocks to map server_name to a root directory and to define access and logging. Typical files live in /etc/nginx/nginx. conf with server blocks in /etc/nginx/conf. d or sites-available. A minimal server block lists listen, server_name, root and an index. The location / block commonly uses try_files to prefer real files and fall back to returning 404. For example, a server block for www. example. com sets root /var/www/example. com/html and access and error log paths. After creating the block test it with nginx -t and reload with systemctl reload nginx. A concrete lab step is to create the document root, add index. html, set ownership to nginx or www-data depending on distro, then confirm curl http://localhost returns the page. A common misconception is copying an Apache Directory directive into Nginx — Nginx handles access rules differently via location and directive scopes. Key takeaway: Nginx server blocks are simple and fast for static assets; always validate syntax and file permissions before relying on them in production.

Securing web traffic with HTTPS is essential. Let's Encrypt provides free certificates and certbot automates obtaining and installing them for Apache and Nginx. The typical flow is: ensure your domain's A record points to the server and that ports 80 and 443 are open; install certbot and the appropriate plugin for your web server; run certbot with the server plugin and domain flags; verify automatic renewal is configured. For Nginx the command is certbot --nginx -d www. example. com -d example. com; for Apache use certbot --apache. Certbot will perform domain validation by reaching your server on port 80, then it will modify server configuration to reference certificate paths and enable HTTPS. Common failures include incorrect DNS, a firewall blocking validation ports, or an existing server block that conflicts with certbot's modifications. After installation, test certificate renewal with certbot renew --dry-run and inspect cron or systemd timers that call renewals. A practical example: after running certbot --nginx, confirm server listens on 443, check the certificate files under /etc/letsencrypt/live, and verify the browser shows a valid HTTPS connection. A common misconception is that certbot automatically fixes every server misconfiguration; in practice you must resolve DNS and conflicting configs first.

Using Nginx as a reverse proxy centralizes TLS termination and allows backend applications to run without direct exposure. The proxy pattern: Nginx receives HTTPS requests, decrypts them, and forwards plain HTTP to a backend app. In a typical setup Nginx listens on 443 with ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key pointing to certbot-managed files, then uses proxy_pass to forward to localhost:3000 or another upstream. It is essential to forward headers like Host, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For so the backend sees the original client address and protocol. Without these headers, backend logs and logic may record requests as coming from 127.0.0.1. Also include proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme when the backend needs to know whether the original request was HTTPS. A concrete example is an app on port 3000 receiving proxied traffic; add the proxy_set_header lines to preserve client identity. Misconceptions include thinking proxy_pass changes the client's IP; it does not unless headers are set. Key takeaway: set headers and test the backend can read them, or client IPs will be lost in logs and analytics. Nginx as a reverse proxy means nginx can terminate tls and forward requests; use proxy_set_header directives so the backend receives the original client information.. Both Apache and Nginx are powerful, but they excel at different tasks. Apache is modular and feature-rich with a long history, making it suitable when you rely on dynamic modules, per-directory. htaccess overrides, or complex rewrites via mod_rewrite. Nginx is event-driven and optimized for high concurrency and static file delivery; it is commonly used as a reverse proxy, load balancer, or cache in front of application servers. In practice, you might use Nginx to terminate TLS and forward to Apache for legacy applications, or choose pure Nginx when low memory and high throughput matter. A common misconception is that one server is always superior; instead, choose based on your app's needs. Example: a high-traffic static asset site benefits from Nginx's performance, while a legacy PHP app relying on many Apache modules may be easier to migrate with Apache. When designing a deployment, consider TLS termination, logging centralization, and whether your backend requires client IPs — if so configure X-Forwarded headers. Key takeaway: pick the server that aligns with workload characteristics and operational constraints, or combine them for best results. Troubleshooting web servers follows a predictable pattern: validate configuration syntax, inspect logs, confirm file permissions, and check network rules. Start with syntax checks: run nginx -t or apachectl configtest to catch parsing errors. If the server fails to start or reload, examine error logs at /var/log/nginx/error. log or /var/log/httpd/error_log to find line numbers and directives causing the failure. Permissions problems often manifest as 403 errors; verify ownership and read permissions for DocumentRoot and log directories and adjust with chown and chmod as needed. On RHEL/CentOS, SELinux can block access even with correct permissions; use restorecon -Rv on your DocumentRoot and setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1 when Nginx must connect to upstream services. Network checks involve ensuring firewall allows HTTP and HTTPS; use firewall-cmd or iptables rules to permit services and then reload. A practical diagnostic flow: run syntax test, tail the error log while reproducing the request, confirm permissions and SELinux context, then verify firewall and DNS. A common misconception is chasing code bugs before confirming that configuration or environment prevents the request from reaching the backend. Close with testing the fix and reloading safely.

Operationalizing web servers in production requires repeatable practices. Always validate configuration changes with nginx -t or apachectl configtest and use graceful reloads to avoid downtime. Automate certificate renewal and monitor certificates so they never expire unexpectedly; certbot sets a timer or cron, and you should confirm it with certbot renew --dry-run. Centralize logs and rotate them to keep disk usage under control and to allow quick forensic analysis. Practice least privilege: the web server user should have only read access to DocumentRoot and write access to log directories; avoid leaving writable file permissions on site folders. When reverse proxying, terminate TLS at the edge and keep internal traffic on a private network when possible. For SELinux-enabled systems, include SELinux context changes in your deployment scripts so restores and policies survive reboots. Finally, document your server blocks and certificate locations so on-call engineers can respond quickly. A misconception is focusing only on feature configuration; operational checks and automation prevent outages. Key takeaway: validate, automate, monitor, and use least privilege to keep web services robust. Third, SSL/TLS with Let's Encrypt and certbot provides free certificates and automated renewal, but certbot requires reachable DNS and open ports for validation.
